title: Inside Elder, Sujan Sarkar's British-Indian Chophouse Reinventing New York Dining
excerpt: The Michelin-starred chef behind Indienne has opened Elder, an à-la-carte British-Indian chophouse at Hudson Yards' Henry Hall — and it may be the clearest sign yet of Indian cuisine's new confidence in America.
body:
• Michelin-starred chef Sujan Sarkar debuted Elder, a British-Indian chophouse, on August 6 at Henry Hall in Hudson Yards — directly below his New York outpost of Indienne.
  • The à-la-carte menu fuses the British chophouse format (chops, fish, puddings, a dedicated potato section) with Indian technique: a pathar kebab hanger steak, Berkshire pork vindaloo rib chop, beet Wellington, and a rasmalai trifle dome.
  • Elder is open Tuesday through Saturday, 5 to 11 p.m. ET; reservations drop 30 days in advance at 9 a.m., and walk-ins are welcome. Weekend brunch service launches later this year.
  • The opening lands as Indian fine dining gains new momentum in New York — and an Indian cocktail bar, Apas, is set to complete Sarkar's Henry Hall trio later this year.

Chef Sujan Sarkar is having a year most restaurateurs would trade a decade for. In May, he brought Indienne — the Chicago restaurant that became the city's first Indian restaurant to earn a Michelin star — to Hudson Yards. On August 6, he opened Elder downstairs in the same building, a British-Indian chophouse that exists, in his own words, in a category that has "never been done before."

Named for the elderflower, which grows in both India and England, Elder is Sarkar's attempt to put two culinary languages on the same table: the working-class London chophouse of his early career and the Indian cooking he grew up with. It is also the latest entry in what is rapidly becoming the most ambitious Indian restaurant portfolio in New York.

A chef's New York homecoming

Sarkar's relationship with New York began nearly a decade ago. In 2017, he opened Baar Baar, a modern Indian restaurant and cocktail bar in the East Village, alongside Roop in Chicago — openings he now considers ahead of their time. (Baar Baar has since closed; a Los Angeles outpost remains.) Before becoming a restaurateur, he spent 11 years in London kitchens, including Automat, and worked at Trèsind in Dubai, according to Resy.

The years since have been a steady build. Indienne opened in Chicago in 2022 and won its Michelin star in 2023. His portfolio now spans Baar Baar LA, the Mediterranean restaurant Sifr in Chicago, Tiya in San Francisco, and Nadu, a regional Indian restaurant in Chicago, all before this summer's New York double-header at Henry Hall.

Elder nearly happened elsewhere. Sarkar toyed with the British-Indian steakhouse idea as far back as 2023, after Indienne's success. "It would've been too soon," he told Resy. He also considered Chicago for Elder, but concluded that New York — the city where modern British rooms like Lord's and Dean's found an audience, and where Korean steakhouse Cote became a sensation — was the right stage. He credits Cote as a "direct reference" for what he hopes to achieve, except with Indian flavors.

The chophouse, with an Indian accent

The concept starts with what a chophouse actually is. "A chophouse is primarily a British concept. You develop chops, and the cuts are made in a particular way," Sarkar told The Hindu. Unlike the American steakhouse, which begins with the steak and builds outward, a chophouse has "a wider appetite" — prime cuts, yes, but also fish, lamb, chicken, duck, vegetables, potatoes, puddings. The meat does not have to dominate.

Crucially, Sarkar is not laying Indian flavor over British food like a second coat of paint. The Scotch egg sits beside the samosa without either becoming a novelty act. First bites include a ravioli-shaped English pea and fava samosa inspired by nimki, the Indian bar snack; quail Scotch eggs; and a chicken liver choux bun sharpened with spiced cherry chutney. The beans on toast arrives over a sourdough kulcha crowned with a poached egg, while a chicken and leek gushtaba — an airy dumpling suspended in cheddar and walnut broth — nods to both a matzo ball and a Kashmiri classic.

The chops and steaks section is where the identity comes through most clearly: a hanger steak modeled on pathar, the stone-ground kebab; a Vindaloo-spiced Berkshire pork chop; lamb chops rubbed with burrah spice; and a 32-day aged, bone-in ribeye. Sauces move between culinary worlds — Varuval pepper sauce, red pepper makhani, horseradish raita, bone marrow nihari gravy. Dover sole comes with curry beurre blanc, and the desserts run from a banana rum baba with jaggery caramel to a rasmalai trifle dome with pistachio ice cream and jalebi crisp.

"Every dish has a reference to India or Britain, but the food is not aggressively Indian. It is not a curry house."

— Sujan Sarkar, chef and owner

The room, designed with interior designer Mapa Mueller, seats about 100 across a circular bar, dining room, and outdoor patio in 3,300 square feet: hunter green walls, walnut wainscoting, velvet banquettes, and Indian textiles evoking an old London club without becoming a period piece. The drinks program follows the same cross-cultural logic — the Elder Gibson and London Fog read as London classics until the sirka brine or Earl Grey-infused gin quietly reveals the Indian thread. "The word 'punch' itself came from India," Sarkar told The Hindu. "We are taking classic cocktails from London and giving them a slight twist. Nothing is over the top."

What Elder says about Indian food in America

There is a larger shift sitting underneath this opening. A generation ago, Indian food in America meant a narrow band of curry-house familiarity. Sarkar grew up, he says, not knowing what pasta was; Britain arrived at culinary pluralism when curry houses became part of everyday eating. In America, he believes, that shift is happening now — and Elder is built for a diner who no longer needs Indian food to explain itself.

The timing supports him. Resy notes that Indian restaurants including Ambassadors Clubhouse, Bungalow, and Kidilum are among the city's most sought-after reservations, while globally inflected steakhouses like Cuerno and Gui have become some of New York's hottest tables. Sarkar acknowledges the meat-forward Indian restaurants that laid the groundwork, but Elder's move is different: not an Indian restaurant borrowing steakhouse form, and not a steakhouse adding Indian spice — a third category, à la carte and unapologetic, that trusts diners to meet it halfway.

A diaspora dining scene comes of age

For Indian-Americans in New York, Elder's significance runs deeper than one ambitious menu. The diaspora has long dined at two tables: the home-cooked one and the special-occasion one, with restaurants in between that rarely attempted both intimacy and ambition at once. Sarkar's Henry Hall project — a Michelin-starred tasting menu upstairs, an à-la-carte chophouse downstairs, and an Indian cocktail bar, Apas, arriving later this year — builds an entire ecosystem where Indian cooking is the house cuisine, not the guest.

That matters for how the next generation cooks, too. In Elder's first days, Sarkar told The Hindu he noticed people from different parts of the world sitting at the same table, eating quite different things — chicken, fish, vegetarian — and everyone was happy. "That is a wonderful experience," he said. It is also a quietly radical image: Indian food as the common ground of a mixed table, rather than the exotic option on it.

What's next

Elder is currently open Tuesday through Saturday, 5 to 11 p.m. Eastern, at Henry Hall in Hudson Yards, with weekend brunch planned for later this year. Sarkar's expansion continues beyond New York: Apas, the Indian cocktail bar, arrives at Henry Hall later in 2026, and he is opening in Abu Dhabi at the end of the year. India remains on the horizon, pending the right place and the right time after an earlier restaurant there was cut short by the COVID-19 pandemic.

"I still think New York is the greatest food city in the world. To be successful in New York, it takes time and patience. But we are not going anywhere."

— Sujan Sarkar, chef and owner

Elder's bet is that the American diner is ready — that a vindaloo rib chop and a hanger steak borrowing from pathar can share a menu without apology. Nine years into cooking in America, Sarkar is done translating. The rest of us get to catch up.
